As of 243 AM EDT Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Surface high pressure is currently stationed across the 
Ohio Valley early this morning with upper level troughing directly 
overhead northern New York and Vermont. Throughout the night, 
temperatures are expected to fall into the mid 50s to mid 60s. This 
will also bring the potential for patchy valley fog, especially in 
Adirondack locations that received rainfall yesterday (portions of 
western Adacks reported 0.50-1.50 inches). Throughout the day 
today, troughing will slide east of the region, but we should 
have enough shortwave energy, moisture, and warmth to allow for 
some showers and thunderstorms, about 25-65% chance in northern 
New York, highest in the northern Adirondacks. For Vermont, 
chances are lower in general, around 5-40%, and mainly in the 
Greens or from any precip that forms in the Adirondacks and 
holds together as it drifts eastward. Should the New York 
locations that received sufficient rainfall yesterday (these 
areas may include Hogansburg, Brasher, Tupper Lake, Parishville,
Horseshoe Lake, South Bombay, Stark, and eastern Potsdam) 
receive another round or two of showers or thunderstorms today 
we'll need to monitor these areas for potential flash flooding, 
but this threat is highly conditional. The Weather Prediction 
Center currently has most of northern New York, outside of the 
Champlain Valley, under a Marginal Risk (Risk level 1 out of 4; 
5% chance for rainfall exceeding flash flood guidance) for 
today. Northern New York rivers could see some small rises, but 
nothing near bankfull with the recent dryness we have had. 
Temperatures today will be in the upper 70s to mid 80s, slightly
above seasonal normals. Tonight, shower activity should dwindle
again like yesterday, and lows will be relatively mild in the 
mid 50s to mid 60s. Total precipitation amounts will be around 
0.10-0.25" in the Adirondacks and parts of the Greens, locally 
higher in heavy, slow moving storms.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A slow moving upper low is expected to track through the 
region midweek, bringing chances of persistent showery weather 
Tuesday through Thursday. On Tuesday, models place the upper low 
somewhere from the southern Ontario-Quebec line to central New York, 
and its associated surface low pressure around eastern Lake Ontario 
and central New York. This multi-layer low pressure is expected to 
move very little Tuesday and Tuesday night, spinning cyclonically 
over the Northeast and drifting slightly eastward. As it does so, it 
will send plumes of moisture into our area, resulting in 
widespread showers and thunderstorms likely for northern New 
York and southern Vermont. Northern Vermont is a little less 
certain, with several models keeping the main slug of rain from 
reaching the Vermont- Canada border and Northeast Kingdom, 
largely due to downsloping off the Green Mountains with a 
southeasterly flow. The main moisture and instability looks to 
be stationed over New York, with ridging anchored over Maine. 
Tuesday will also be one more chance for temperatures to reach 
the upper 70s and 80s before the system wicks away our warmth, 
which will help fuel any thunderstorms. Models are suggesting 
Pwats could reach as high as 1.75-2.00 inches in some locations,
and surface instability runs around 1500 J/kg, producing tall, 
skinny CAPE soundings. At times, storm motions look to run under
10 knots, indicating any showers or storms could be slow 
moving, heavy rainers. Forecast additional precipitation amounts
from early Tuesday morning into late Tuesday night will be as 
high as 0.50-1.00" Adirondacks and west as well as portions of 
southern Vermont. For the northern Champlain Valley as well as 
northern Vermont and southeastern Vermont, we're looking at 
closer to 0.05- 0.50". At the moment, the most likely 24 hour 
period for the St. Lawrence Valley to get 1 inch is Tuesday and 
Tuesday night. Any areas that see heavier downpours today will 
need to be especially watched on Tuesday. The WPC has a Marginal
(at least 5%) Risk of excessive rainfall over the entire 
forecast area Tuesday.

On Wednesday, the multi-layer low pressure swings southeast into the 
mid-Atlantic, continuing southeasterly to even easterly flow at 
times across the forecast area. Precipitation continues to look more 
likely in southern portions of the forecast area with downsloping in 
the wider valleys, and we lose the majority of instability. Our 
highs only reaching the upper 60s to mid 70s, we won't see the same 
convective showers and storms that we're expecting Tuesday. Still, 
steadier rain could produce as much as 0.75-1.25" of additional rain 
in southern Vermont, with 0.30-0.75" elsewhere. Wednesday is another

excessive rainfall. River rises will be expected by Wednesday night
